subject: Banking
title: Risk-Based Pricing
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Risk-Based Pricing.

hook.text: Two people applying for the same loan get different rates. Your risk profile determines your price.

buildup.text: A borrower with a 780 score gets 6.5% on a mortgage. A borrower with 620 gets 8%. Same loan, different price.

discovery.text: Risk-based pricing means lenders charge more to riskier borrowers to compensate for higher expected default rates.

twist.text: Higher rates on riskier borrowers make them more likely to default.

climax.text: Risk-based pricing is logical for lenders but punitive for borrowers.

punchline.text: Higher risk means higher rates. Those who can least afford it pay the most.

quiz.question: What is risk-based pricing?
options: Interest rates vary based on borrower risk profile

details.summary: Risk-based pricing means that lenders charge different interest rates to different borrowers based on their perceived risk of default. Higher-risk borrowers pay higher rates to compensate the lender for the greater probability of loss.
details.whyItMatters: Risk-based pricing determines why two people buying identical homes pay vastly different amounts over a mortgage's life. A 1 percent rate difference on a 30-year mortgage can mean over 50,000 dollars in additional interest cost.
takeaways: Borrowers with lower credit scores receive higher interest rates
Risk tiers create dramatic differences in total borrowing costs
A small score improvement can move you to a better pricing tier

faq.question: How much difference does a higher credit score make in interest rates?
faq.answer: On a 300,000 dollar 30-year mortgage, the difference between a 620 and 760 credit score can mean 1 to 2 percentage points higher interest, translating to 50,000 to over 100,000 dollars more paid over the loan's life.

faq.question: Is risk-based pricing fair?
faq.answer: Proponents say it allows more people to access credit, since without it, lenders would simply reject high-risk applicants. Critics argue it punishes people already in financial difficulty with higher costs, making their situation worse.
